sections.history: Achirupakkam lies on the highway south of Chengalpattu, in the Thondai country. In the Tevaram the village is Tiruvachirupakkam, and its Shiva temple is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by the child-saint Tirugnanasambandar. The name of the Lord, Atcheeswarar, and the name of the village are both tied to a single incident, the breaking of an axle, 'achu' in Tamil, in the legend told below. Temple accounts call the shrine very old, and it is placed in the Tevaram age, the seventh century. The later patrons of the structure are not firmly recorded in the sources found, but the temple has remained in unbroken worship, and the village still carries the story in its name.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is entered beneath a five-tiered gateway. Its most distinctive feature is that the Lord is honoured in two sanctums: Atcheeswarar, a self-manifested linga facing east, and Umayatcheeswarar in a second sanctum. In the same way two goddesses are worshipped in shrines of their own, Ilangili Ammai and Umayambigai. Outside the temple, facing west, stands the shrine of Achumuri Vinayaka, the Vinayaka of the broken axle, to whom devotees pray to overcome obstacles. The poet-saint Arunagirinathar is said to have sung of him in the Tiruppugazh as Achiru Vinayaka.
sections.legends: The village is bound to the story of the burning of the three cities. Setting out to destroy the demons of Tripura, Shiva mounted his chariot without first praying to Vinayaka, the remover of obstacles, and at this place the chariot's axle broke. Realising the omission, the Lord worshipped Vinayaka, who mended the axle, and Shiva went on to his victory. The spot where the axle broke is remembered as Achirupakkam, and the Lord here is Atcheeswarar, the Lord of the Axle. A second tradition tells that the axle of a Pandya king's chariot, as he travelled to bring earth from the Ganga for a dam on a nearby river, broke here as well. The lesson of both tales is the same: no undertaking, not even Shiva's, should begin without the blessing of Vinayaka.
sections.festivals: The principal annual festival is the ten-day Chithirai Brahmotsavam in April or May. Special worship is offered on new-moon and full-moon days, and Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at Shiva temples generally. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Achirupakkam is an easy and rewarding stop for pilgrims travelling the highway south from Chennai. Begin, as the legend itself teaches, at the shrine of Achumuri Vinayaka outside the temple, then enter to the sanctum of Atcheeswarar and the second sanctum of Umayatcheeswarar, and visit the two goddesses in their own shrines. Many who come pray for obstacles to be lifted from a new beginning, which is precisely the grace the story of the axle recalls. The temple is quiet outside festival days, and the pairing of two sanctums for one Lord gives the visit a character found in few other shrines.

visit.timings: Commonly reported as open from about 6:00 to 12:00 in the morning and 4:00 to 8:00 in the evening, though listings differ slightly; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Achirupakkam stands on the Chennai–Tindivanam highway (the GST Road), about 96 km from Chennai, in Madurantakam taluk of Chengalpattu district. Chengalpattu, roughly 40 km to the north, has the nearest major railway junction, and Chennai International Airport is about 80 km away. Buses along the highway stop at Achirupakkam, and the temple is in the town.
